conceptTag: Build a brand for a business supplier
readerTitle: Chefs don't buy your logo. They buy a calm Saturday night.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 대상 채소 도매업체, 가구 제조사의 사내 IT 지원팀) · 적용 레슨: 브랜드 약속(MKT-02-02)과 브랜드 신뢰(MKT-02-05)를 기업 고객을 상대하는 공급자에게 적용
insight: 기업 고객에게 브랜드는 로고가 아니라 '이 공급자가 내 하루를 편하게 해 줄까'에 대한 예측이다. 그 예측은 지킬 수 있는 약속 하나와, 약속을 어긴 날의 대처로 만들어진다.
misconception: B2B 공급자의 브랜드 작업은 로고, 트럭 도색, 웹사이트를 새로 다듬는 일이다. 문제가 생긴 날은 조용히 넘기는 편이 브랜드에 낫다.

sources.text: 모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시
이 유닛의 개념 레슨: MKT-02-02 브랜드 약속, MKT-02-05 브랜드 신뢰

factChecks.note: Harbor Produce와 가구 제조사 IT팀은 모두 가상 사례입니다. 실제 기업 이름, 통계, 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다. 같은 이름의 실제 업체가 있는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
가상 수치 일관성 확인: 거래처 40곳, 약속 '밤 10시 주문, 오전 7시 도착, 놓치면 그 배송분 무료', 4시 30분 트럭 고장, 영향 받는 주방 12곳, 예상 도착 9시 30분(2시간 30분 지연). 카드 2·4·5에서 숫자가 같은지 다시 확인하세요.
softwareNote의 상태 페이지·장애 안내 내용은 일반적인 관행으로만 서술했고 효과에 대한 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Chefs don't buy your logo. They buy a calm Saturday night.
body: Harbor Produce delivers vegetables to 40 restaurants. Its trucks are clean, its logo is fine, and its prices match two local rivals.

The owner wants more kitchens to choose Harbor. Most of her ideas start with a new look. Her customers care about something else: what happens at 5 p.m. on a busy Saturday, when the tomatoes should already be there.

image.label: A chef checking an empty shelf in a busy kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저녁 영업 직전 바쁜 레스토랑 주방, 셰프가 빈 채소 선반을 보며 시계를 확인하는 장면. 뒤편 창밖에 배송 트럭이 살짝 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Harbor put its brand money first?
body: You own Harbor. You have a modest budget to make restaurants pick you over the two rivals. What do you do first?

options.text: Refresh the logo, wrap the trucks and rebuild the website
options.feedback: You'd look sharper, but chefs would still see three interchangeable suppliers. New paint gives them no reason to switch.

options.text: Pick one promise chefs can plan around, like "ordered by 10 p.m., in your kitchen by 7 a.m.", and run the business to keep it
options.feedback: This is the **brand promise** at work: one specific thing buyers can count on, which also tells your team what to protect. It costs more to run, as you'll see.

options.text: Claim it all: widest range, lowest prices, local and organic
options.feedback: Each claim may be partly true, but a list is hard to remember and harder to keep. Rivals say the same things, so none of it sticks.

cards.title: A business buyer's job is on the line.
body: When a chef picks a supplier, their own customers, staff and reviews depend on that choice. A missing crate is their problem first.

So a supplier's brand is mostly a forecast in the buyer's head: **will this company make my day easier or harder?** That forecast is shaped by delivery times, invoices and phone calls far more than by colors.
That's why a clear promise matters so much. It gives the chef something to plan around.

cards.title: A promise only works if daily work keeps it.
body: Harbor's promise looks like one sentence. Behind it sit real changes to how the business runs.

breakdown.label: The promise
breakdown.detail: Ordered by 10 p.m., in your kitchen by 7 a.m. Miss it, and that delivery is free.

breakdown.label: What chefs hear
breakdown.detail: I can plan my morning around this supplier.

breakdown.label: What it takes
breakdown.detail: Routes set the night before, earlier loading, a spare driver on call.

breakdown.label: The proof
breakdown.detail: A monthly on-time record sent to every customer.

cards.callout: The promise is also an instruction to your own team.
cards.softwareNote: For a software supplier, the same idea is a specific commitment like uptime or support reply times, backed by the staffing and tooling needed to keep it.

cards.title: A truck breaks down at 4:30 a.m.
body: The 7 a.m. promise is six months old and mostly kept. Today one truck fails. Twelve kitchens will get their order around 9:30.

options.text: Rush the deliveries and apologise when the driver arrives
options.feedback: Speed matters, but chefs discover the gap at 7 a.m. with empty shelves. They lose two hours they could have spent re-planning.

options.text: Text all 12 kitchens by 5:30 with the new time, and credit the delivery as promised
options.feedback: **Brand trust** at work: the promise broke, but your response proved you mean it. Chefs can adjust prep, and the credit shows the guarantee is real.

options.text: Say nothing. One late morning in six months is fine
options.feedback: It saves an awkward message, but chefs find the miss themselves. Now they doubt the promise on every other day too.

cards.title: Trust is built on the bad days.
body: Business buyers know problems happen. What they remember is whether they heard it from you first, and whether you did what you said you would.
An early warning turns a failure into evidence that the promise is taken seriously. A surprise turns it into evidence that it isn't.

image.label: Phone showing an early delivery-delay text to a chef
image.brief: 새벽 5시 30분, 주방 조리대 위 휴대폰 화면에 "Your delivery will arrive at 9:30. Today's order is on us." 문자. 옆에 셰프가 메모지에 준비 순서를 다시 적는 손. 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.softwareNote: In software, this is the status page and the outage email. A note sent before customers notice keeps the promise visible even when the product fails.

cards.title: A promise is a cost you pay every day.
body: Harbor's 7 a.m. promise needs a spare driver and earlier loading. That money is spent whether or not anything goes wrong.

And a promise broken every week does more harm than no promise at all, because buyers now have a number to hold you to. Start with something you already keep almost every day. Tighten it only once the operation can carry it.

cards.title: Now you're a team inside a company.
body: You lead IT support at a furniture manufacturer. Other departments call you slow, and some now buy their own software without telling you. The finance director asks you to fix the team's reputation.

options.text: Rename the team, launch a new intranet page and host a "meet IT" coffee morning
options.feedback: It builds goodwill, but nothing changes in what colleagues experience. Their forecast of your team stays the same.

options.text: Promise one thing: every request gets a named person and a reply within four working hours. Share the monthly record, misses included
options.feedback: A clear **brand promise** colleagues can plan around, plus **brand trust** from showing the misses honestly. Internal customers are still customers.

options.text: Promise to say yes to every request, faster than before
options.feedback: It sounds generous, but no team can keep it. The first broken yes confirms the reputation you're trying to change.

cards.title: A supplier's brand is a promise kept, even on bad days.
list: **The brand promise:** one specific thing buyers can plan around
**Brand trust:** keep it visibly, and handle misses before customers find them
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write the one sentence a customer could repeat about what you guarantee. Then write what you'll do on the day you miss it.
